home.title: Everything attracts.
home.description: Experiment with gravity, test your intuition, and discover the surprising dance of three bodies. No physics background needed.

orbits.title: Order in motion.
orbits.description: Three bodies. One law. Six extraordinary ways to return to the beginning. Choose an orbit and follow the journey.
orbits.note: These are not hand-drawn curves: trajectories are generated from published initial conditions and numerically validated.
orbits.conceptText: Each body attracts the other two. With very specific initial conditions, their positions and velocities return to the starting point.
orbits.planar: Planar orbit · The 3D camera changes your perspective, not the physics.

lagrange.name: Lagrange
lagrange.subtitle: Symmetry in motion

figure-eight.name: Figure eight
figure-eight.subtitle: One curve, three travelers
figure-eight.description: Three equal masses follow the same figure eight, separated by one third of the period.

butterfly-i.name: Butterfly I

goggles.name: Goggles
goggles.subtitle: Interwoven loops
goggles.description: Three bodies trace connected loops that repeat after one period.

moth-i.name: Moth I
moth-i.subtitle: A delicate dynamic balance

yin-yang-i.name: Yin-Yang I

yin-yang-i.description: A periodic solution with central symmetry and close passages between bodies.

learn.title: Gravity starts with two.
learn.description: You do not need to memorize a formula. Move the masses, change the distance, and watch what happens.
learn.formulaText: Force F increases with masses m₁ and m₂ and decreases with the square of center-to-center distance r. G is the universal gravitational constant.
learn.equal: Equal magnitude, opposite directions. Acceleration is F/m: the smaller mass accelerates more.
learn.scale: Body radii and arrows are illustrative; force values are calculated in SI units.
learn.predictionTitle: Before you try it, what do you predict?
learn.predictionQuestion: If we double the distance and keep the masses, the force becomes…
learn.correct: Exactly. Doubling r multiplies r² by four, so the force becomes one quarter.
learn.incorrect: The force becomes one quarter: distance is squared, and 2² = 4.
learn.nextTitle: What if we add a third body?
learn.nextText: Every pair follows this same law. Their interactions create complex motion and, in special cases, repeating orbits.
learn.predictionHint: Choose an answer, then check its effect in the laboratory.
